lessons.title: Lesson 18: Present Progressive ~고 있다; To be Getting ~아/어지다

grammar.explanation:
~고 있다 says an action is happening right now, like English "I am ___ing". The plain present 먹어요 can also mean "I'm eating", so use ~고 있다 when you want to stress that the action is in progress at this moment.

To form it, add ~고 있다 to the verb stem, then conjugate 있다 as usual. The stem never changes, because ~고 starts with a consonant: 먹다 → 먹 + 고 있어요 → 먹고 있어요; 자르다 → 자르 + 고 있어요 → 자르고 있어요; 공부하다 → 공부하 + 고 있어요 → 공부하고 있어요.

Tense goes on 있다, not on the main verb: 하고 있었어요 (was doing). For someone you honor, such as parents or a teacher, use 계시다 instead of 있다: 보고 계세요.

~고 있다 only works with action verbs. You can't say 춥고 있어요 for "it is being cold". To talk about an adjective changing, use ~아/어지다 (below).

examples.en: The monkey is eating a banana.
I am reading a novel now.
My friend is cutting paper with scissors.
Last night I was doing homework.
My parents are watching TV in the living room.
examples.note: 계시다 is the honorific form of 있다, used here because the subject is parents.

grammar.point: 살고 있다 / 알고 있다 / 가지고 있다
grammar.explanation:
Some verbs describe a situation that continues over time rather than a single action: living somewhere, knowing something, owning something. Korean often puts these in the ~고 있다 form, even though English uses the simple present ("I live", "I know", "I have").

Form them like any ~고 있다 verb: 살다 → 살 + 고 있어요 → 살고 있어요; 알다 → 알 + 고 있어요 → 알고 있어요; 가지다 → 가지 + 고 있어요 → 가지고 있어요. The ㄹ in 살다 and 알다 stays, because ㄹ only drops before ㄴ, ㅂ and ㅅ.

The plain forms 살아요, 알아요 and 가져요 mean nearly the same thing. 알고 있어요 often adds a sense of "I already know", and 가지고 있어요 is much more common than 가져요 for "I have (it with me)". In the past, 살고 있었어요 means "I was living there (at that time)".

examples.en: Last year I was living in Busan.
Do you know that singer's name?
I have a map of Korea.

grammar.explanation:
앉다 (to sit down), 서다 (to stand up) and 눕다 (to lie down) describe the movement of getting into a position. To describe the state you are in afterwards (being seated, standing or lying), use ~아/어 있다.

Make the 아/어 form you already use for 아/어요, then add 있다: 앉다 → 앉 + 아 있다 → 앉아 있어요 (stem vowel ㅏ, so 아); 서다 → 서 + 어 있다 → 서 있어요 (서 + 어 merges to 서); 눕다 → 누우 + 어 있다 → 누워 있어요 (ㅂ irregular). Tense goes on 있다: 앉아 있었어요 means "was sitting". For honored people, use 계시다: 앉아 계세요.

Don't use ~고 있다 here by mistake. 앉고 있어요 means you are in the middle of sitting down, not that you are seated.

The same pattern describes the result of other changes too, such as 열리다 (to be opened): 문이 열려 있어요 means "the door is open".

examples.en: The students are sitting on chairs.
The teacher is standing in front of the desk.
The child is lying on the bed.

examples.ko: 어제 버스에서 한 시간 동안 서 있었어요.
examples.en: Yesterday I stood on the bus for an hour.
Grandma is sitting in the living room.
examples.note: Honored subject, so 있다 becomes 계시다: 앉아 계세요.
열리다 + 어 있다 → 열려 있어요: the state left after the door was opened.

grammar.explanation:
Adjectives describe a state: 추워요 means "it is cold". To talk about a change into that state, "to get cold" or "to become clean", add ~아/어지다 to the adjective stem. The result is a verb, so it takes all tenses and can even take ~고 있다.

Make the same 아/어 form as for 아/어요, then add 지다 with no space: 좋다 → 좋 + 아지다 → 좋아지다 (ㅗ stem, so 아); 밝다 → 밝아지다; 깨끗하다 → 깨끗해지다 (하 + 여 → 해); 춥다 → 추워지다 (ㅂ irregular); 크다 → 커지다 (ㅡ drops).

Compare: 날씨가 추워요 (it is cold), 날씨가 추워져요 (it gets cold), 날씨가 추워졌어요 (it got cold), 날씨가 추워지고 있어요 (it is getting colder right now). Never put ~고 있다 straight on an adjective, as in 춥고 있어요.

You saw ~아/어지다 on verbs in Lesson 14, where it makes a passive. On adjectives it means "to become".

examples.en: The sky gets brighter at dawn.

examples.note: 어둡다 is ㅂ irregular: 어둡 + 어지다 → 어두워지다.

examples.en: My younger sibling has gotten a lot taller.
examples.note: 크다 drops ㅡ: 크 + 어지다 → 커지다.

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Korean Comparatives and Superlatives: 더, 보다, 가장/제일

grammar.explanation:
더 means "more". Korean adjectives have no special "-er" form, so 더 does the job of both "more" and "-er": 더 넓어요 (is wider), 더 비싸요 (is more expensive).

Put 더 directly before the adjective or verb it affects. With verbs it means doing something more or to a greater degree: 더 좋아해요 (like more), 더 먹고 싶어요 (want to eat more). With a 하다 verb, 더 goes before the whole verb (더 공부해요), or before 하다 when the noun takes ~을/를 (공부를 더 해요). 조금 더 means "a little more".

You don't have to say what you're comparing with. If the context is clear, 이 방이 더 넓어요 simply means "this room is bigger (than the other one)". To name the other thing, add ~보다 (next point).

examples.en: I want to eat more ramen.
Please give me a little more.

grammar.explanation:
~보다 means "than". Attach it directly to the noun you are comparing against. It has the same shape after vowels and consonants: 저 + 보다 → 저보다; 영어 + 보다 → 영어보다; 어제 + 보다 → 어제보다.

The usual order is: A이/가 B보다 (더) adjective, meaning "A is more ___ than B". Because ~보다 already shows the comparison, 더 is optional. The ~보다 phrase can also come first: 영어보다 한국어가 어려워요 means the same as 한국어가 영어보다 어려워요.

A common mistake is putting ~보다 on the wrong noun. The noun with ~보다 is the one with less of the quality. In 서울이 부산보다 커요, Seoul is the bigger city. ~보다 can also attach to time words: 어제보다 (than yesterday), 평소보다 (than usual).

examples.en: My younger sibling is taller than me.
This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
I like Korean food more than Western food.
This road is narrower than that road.
Today I'm more tired than usual.

grammar.explanation:
덜 means "less". It is the opposite of 더 and sits in the same place, right before the adjective or verb: 덜 추워요 (is less cold), 덜 먹어요 (eat less). It combines with ~보다 the same way: 오늘은 어제보다 덜 추워요.

English often says "not as ___" or uses the opposite adjective, but Korean uses 덜 freely. 덜 매워요 (less spicy) is a natural way to talk about milder food.

Don't confuse 덜 with 안. 덜 means a smaller amount or degree; 안 means "not at all". 덜 매워요 is "less spicy", but 안 매워요 is "not spicy".

examples.en: Today is less cold than yesterday.
I am less lazy than my older brother.
These days I drink less coffee.

grammar.explanation:
가장 and 제일 both mean "the most" and make superlatives. Put either one right before the adjective or verb: 제일 좋아요 (is the best), 가장 커요 (is the biggest), 제일 좋아해요 (like the most).

제일 is the everyday spoken choice. 가장 sounds a bit more formal and is common in writing, but both are correct anywhere.

To say "in" or "among" a group, put ~에서 or ~중에서 after the group: 우리 반 + 에서 → 우리 반에서 (in our class); 과일 + 중에서 → 과일 중에서 (among fruits). The winner usually takes ~이/가, because it is the new information: 과일 중에서 사과가 제일 맛있어요.

Superlatives also work before a noun with the ~ㄴ/은 form: 제일 추운 날 (the coldest day).

examples.ko: 우리 반에서 민수가 키가 가장 커요.
examples.en: Minsu is the tallest in our class.
Among fruits, apples are the tastiest.

examples.note: 제일 can come before an adjective that describes a noun: 제일 추운 날.

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Well and Poorly: 잘 and 못

vocab.en: to gain, to improve, to increase
to escape, to come out of
to escape, to go out of
to be round, to be spherical

grammar.explanation:
잘하다 means "to be good at" and 못하다 means "to be bad at". The skill is a noun marked with ~을/를: 수영을 잘해요 (I'm good at swimming), 요리를 못해요 (I'm bad at cooking).

Both are single words written without a space, and they conjugate like any 하다 verb: 잘하 + 여요 → 잘해요, past 잘했어요; 못하 + 여요 → 못해요, past 못했어요. With an honored subject: 잘하세요.

Watch the spacing. 요리를 못해요 (one word) says you are bad at cooking as a skill. 요리를 못 해요 (two words) says you can't cook, for example because there's no time. They sound the same, so context decides.

잘하다 can also be used without an object to mean "to do well": 그 팀은 정말 잘했어요.

examples.en: My older brother is bad at sports.
That team did really well yesterday.
Are your parents good at driving?

grammar.explanation:
잘 is an adverb meaning "well". Put it directly before the verb, which doesn't change: 자다 → 잘 자요 (sleep well); 먹다 → 잘 먹었어요 (I ate well); 가르치다 → 잘 가르쳐요.

With a 하다 verb, put 잘 before the whole verb (잘 번역해요), or turn the noun into an object and use 잘하다 (번역을 잘해요). Both mean "translates well".

잘 often means "properly" or "carefully" rather than "skillfully". You'll hear it in many set phrases: 잘 지내요? (Are you doing well?), 잘 먹겠습니다 (said before a meal), 잘 들으세요 (listen carefully).

To say something isn't done well, use 잘 못 + verb (see 잘못 vs 잘 못 below).

examples.en: Listen carefully to what I say.
examples.note: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣 + 으세요 → 들으세요.

examples.en: Did you do well on the test yesterday?

grammar.explanation:
못 before a verb means "can't" or "couldn't". Use it when you want to do something but are unable to, because of skill, time, health or other circumstances. 안 is different: 안 가요 means you aren't going (maybe by choice), while 못 가요 means you can't go.

Place 못 right before the verb, which conjugates normally: 가다 → 못 가요, past 못 갔어요; 먹다 → 못 먹어요. With 하다 verbs made from a noun, 못 goes between the noun and 하다: 운전하다 → 운전 못 해요; 숙제하다 → 숙제를 못 했어요. Saying 못 운전해요 is a common mistake.

Pronunciation: before ㅁ or ㄴ, 못 sounds like 몬: 못 먹어요 sounds like [몬머거요]. 못 goes with verbs only; for adjectives use 안 or ~지 않다.

examples.en: I can't go to school today.
I couldn't do my homework yesterday.

examples.note: With a 하다 verb, 못 goes between the noun and 하다.

grammar.explanation:
~지 못하다 means the same as 못 + verb: "can't" or "couldn't". It is a little more formal and very common in writing and the news, but you'll hear it in speech too. It's the "can't" partner of ~지 않다 from Lesson 8.

Form it by adding ~지 to the stem and then 못하다 (one word, conjugated like any 하다 verb). The stem never changes: 가다 → 가 + 지 못해요 → 가지 못해요; 먹다 → 먹지 못해요; 번역하다 → 번역하지 못해요. Tense goes on 못하다: 가지 못했어요 (couldn't go).

Compare the pairs: 안 가요 = 가지 않아요 (don't go); 못 가요 = 가지 못해요 (can't go). With long 하다 verbs, ~지 못하다 avoids splitting the verb: 이해하지 못했어요 instead of 이해 못 했어요.

examples.en: I can't go to class today.
I couldn't understand what that person said.

grammar.explanation:
Spacing changes the meaning here. 잘못 (one word) is a noun meaning "mistake" or "fault", or an adverb meaning "wrongly, by mistake". 잘 못 (two words) is 잘 (well) + 못 (can't): "can't do well".

As a noun, 잘못 takes particles and 이다: 제 잘못이에요 (it's my fault). As an adverb it goes right before the verb: 잘못 탔어요 (took the wrong one), 잘못 썼어요 (wrote it wrong). There is also the verb 잘못하다, "to do wrong": 제가 잘못했어요 is a common apology.

잘 못 + verb says you can do something, but not well: 노래를 잘 못 불러요 (I can't sing well). In speech the two sound alike, so listen to the rest of the sentence: is it about a mistake, or about skill?

examples.en: I was wrong. / It's my fault.
I wrote the phone number wrong.

examples.note: 부르다 is 르 irregular: 부르 + 어요 → 불러요.

lessons.title: Lesson 21: Asking Questions in Korean: Why, When, Where, Who

vocab.en: to check out of a hospital
to not be enough, to be lacking

grammar.explanation:
In Korean, a yes/no question looks exactly like a statement. 밥 먹었어요. means "I ate." Say 밥 먹었어요? with your voice rising at the end and it means "Did you eat?" There is no extra word like "do" and no change in word order.

This works with every ending you know: present 가요?, past 갔어요?, future 갈 거예요?, and casual 가? The subject "you" is usually dropped because it's obvious who you're asking.

Answer with 네 (yes) or 아니요 (no). Be careful with negative questions: 네 agrees with what was said, not with the verb. If someone asks 커피 안 마셔요? (Don't you drink coffee?), 네, 안 마셔요 means "Right, I don't."

examples.en: Are you going to school tomorrow?
Will you go to the wedding tomorrow?

examples.note: 네 agrees with the negative question, so it means "right, I don't".

grammar.explanation:
~ㅂ/습니까 is the question form of the formal ~ㅂ/습니다 ending. Use it in the most formal situations: interviews, announcements, speaking to customers, or in the army. In everyday conversation, the polite 요 form with a rising tone is more common.

After a vowel stem, add ~ㅂ니까: 가다 → 가 + ㅂ니까 → 갑니까; 간단하다 → 간단합니까. After a consonant stem, add ~습니까: 있다 → 있습니까; 먹다 → 먹습니까. A ㄹ stem drops the ㄹ and takes ~ㅂ니까: 살다 → 삽니까. For 이다, use 입니까: 학생입니까?

For the past, add it to the past stem. That stem always ends in ㅆ, so it's always ~습니까: 갔 + 습니까 → 갔습니까. Answer formally with ~ㅂ/습니다: 네, 있습니다.

examples.en: Did you go to the wedding yesterday?

examples.note: 살다 drops ㄹ: 살 + ㅂ니까 → 삽니까.

examples.en: Are you going on a business trip tomorrow?

grammar.explanation:
~니 makes a casual question in 반말. It sounds warm and a little soft, and adults often use it with children or close friends. Don't use it with people older than you or with strangers. The plain 반말 question (먹었어?) is the other casual option.

Attach ~니 directly to the stem, with no 아/어: 먹다 → 먹 + 니 → 먹니?; 가다 → 가니? For the past, add it to the past stem: 먹었 + 니 → 먹었니? For the future: 갈 거 + 니 → 갈 거니?

A ㄹ stem drops the ㄹ: 살다 → 사니?, 알다 → 아니? (careful: this sounds like 아니, "no"). With 이다, use 이니 after a consonant and just 니 after a vowel: 학생이니?, 누구니? It works with adjectives too: 배고프니?

examples.en: Are you reading a comic book?
Are you going to school tomorrow?

examples.note: After a vowel, 이다 + 니 shortens to just 니: 누구니.

grammar.explanation:
~ㄴ/은가요 asks a question more softly than the plain 요 form. It sounds gentle and a little indirect, as if you're wondering out loud, so it's polite with strangers or people above you. Without 요 it's casual.

It attaches to adjectives and 이다 in the present tense, using the same shape as the adjective-before-noun form (Lesson 4). After a vowel, add ~ㄴ가요: 비싸다 → 비싼가요; 이다 → 인가요 (선생님인가요). After a consonant, add ~은가요: 좁다 → 좁은가요. A ㄹ stem drops ㄹ: 길다 → 긴가요. ㅂ irregulars change: 어렵다 → 어려운가요.

Words ending in 있다 or 없다 (재미있다, 맛없다) don't use this; they take ~나요 instead (재미있나요?). Verbs and past tenses also take ~나요 (next point).

examples.note: 어렵다 is ㅂ irregular: 어렵 + 은가요 → 어려운가요.
길다 drops ㄹ: 길 + ㄴ가요 → 긴가요.

grammar.explanation:
~나요 is the soft question ending for verbs and for 있다/없다 (including 재미있다, 맛있다). Like ~ㄴ/은가요, it sounds gentle and polite, a bit like "I wonder...". Without 요 it's casual.

Attach ~나요 straight to the stem, whether it ends in a vowel or a consonant: 가다 → 가나요; 먹다 → 먹나요; 있다 → 있나요. A ㄹ stem drops the ㄹ: 알다 → 아나요, 살다 → 사나요.

For the past, add ~나요 to the past stem: 갔 + 나요 → 갔나요; 퇴원했나요. This works for past adjectives too: 비쌌나요?

Rule of thumb: present adjective or 이다 → ~ㄴ/은가요. Verb, 있다/없다, or any past tense → ~나요.

examples.en: Has your friend already left the hospital?
Did it rain a lot yesterday?

examples.note: Past adjectives take ~나요, not ~은가요.

grammar.explanation:
왜 means "why". It's an adverb, so you don't change the sentence. Just add 왜 to a normal question, usually at the start or right before the verb: 늦었어요? → 왜 늦었어요?

It combines freely with negatives and other forms you know: 왜 안 와요? (Why aren't you coming?), 왜 못 왔어요? (Why couldn't you come?), 왜 가고 싶어요? (Why do you want to go?).

On its own, 왜? means "What?" when someone calls your name, and 왜요? is a polite "Why?" when you're surprised. Said sharply, 왜 can sound like a challenge, so tone matters.

examples.en: Why does that person regret it?
Why do you want to go to Korea?

grammar.explanation:
언제 means "when". Put it where the time word would go in the answer: 내일 졸업해요 → 언제 졸업해요? Unlike time words such as 내일, 언제 normally takes no ~에.

Other particles can attach to it: 언제부터 (since when), 언제까지 (until when). With 이다 it asks for a date or time. 언제 ends in a vowel, so it takes 예요: 생일이 언제예요?

For a clock time, ask with 몇 시 (Lesson 22) instead: 몇 시에 만나요? 언제 is more general and asks which day, which week or which time of year.

examples.en: Until when are you in the hospital?
When did you come to Korea?
Since when have you studied Korean?

grammar.explanation:
어디 means "where". It sits where the place would be in the answer, and takes the same particle the place would take: ~에 for going or being somewhere (어디에 가요?, 어디에 있어요?), and ~에서 for doing an action somewhere (어디에서 공부해요?). Add ~에서 for "from where" too: 어디에서 왔어요?

In speech, ~에 is often dropped (어디 가요?), and 어디에서 shortens to 어디서.

To ask where a place is, use 이다. 어디 ends in a vowel, so it's 어디예요: 화장실이 어디예요? To ask where a person or object is, use 있다: 지갑이 어디에 있어요?

누구 means "who". It acts like a noun, so it goes where the person would be in the answer and takes the same particles: 누구를 만났어요? (object), 누구예요? (with 이다), 누구한테 전화했어요? (to whom), 누구하고 살아요? (with whom). Before another noun it means "whose": 누구 가방이에요? (Whose bag is it?)

As the subject, 누구 + 가 contracts to 누가: 누가 왔어요? Never say 누구가. A question word is new information, so it never takes ~은/는.

In speech, 누구를 is often shortened to 누굴.

examples.note: 누구 directly before a noun means "whose".

lessons.title: Lesson 22: Asking Questions in Korean: How, What, Which, How Many

vocab.en: a seat, a place to put something
to collect, to come and pick up
to go and then come back
to be short, to be brief

grammar.explanation:
어떻게 means "how", in the sense of "in what way" or "by what method". It's an adverb made from 어떻다 (to be how), and it goes right before the verb: 어떻게 읽어요? (How do you read it?), 어떻게 가요? (How do you get there?).

Answer with a method. For transport, use ~(으)로 from Lesson 12: 버스로 가요. To ask how to say something in a language, use ~(으)로 too: 한국어로 어떻게 말해요?

Don't confuse 어떻게 with 어때요. 어떻게 + verb asks about a method; 어때요 asks for an opinion ("How is it?"). Also useful: 어떻게 해요? means "What do I do?" when something has gone wrong.

examples.en: How do you read this word?
How do you get to school?
How do you make this food?
How do you say this in Korean?
How did you get home yesterday?
How do you attach this file?

grammar.explanation:
어때요 is the 요 form of 어떻다 ("to be how"). Use it to ask for an opinion or impression: "How is it?", "What do you think of it?" It also makes suggestions: 내일 어때요? (How about tomorrow?)

어떻다 is ㅎ irregular, which Lesson 23 covers: 어떻 + 어요 → 어때요; past 어떻 + 었어요 → 어땠어요. The casual forms are 어때? and 어땠어?

Put the thing you're asking about first, with ~이/가, ~은/는 or no particle: 날씨가 어때요?, 이 치마 어때요? Answer with an adjective: 좋아요, 괜찮아요. Remember: 어때요 stands at the end on its own, while 어떻게 comes before a verb.

examples.en: How about a cup of coffee?

grammar.explanation:
뭐 and 무엇 both mean "what". They are pronouns, so they take the place of the unknown thing, with whatever particle it would have. 무엇 is formal or written and pairs with ~ㅂ/습니까; 뭐 is the spoken form.

The particles contract in speech. Subject: 무엇이 → 뭐가 (뭐가 맛있어요?). Object: 무엇을 → 뭘 or 뭐를, or just 뭐 with no particle (뭐 먹어요?). With 이다: 뭐 + 예요 → 뭐예요? (전공이 뭐예요?)

Use 뭐 for "what" on its own. When "what" comes right before a noun ("what food"), use 무슨 instead (next point). In casual speech, 뭐? alone means "What?"

examples.en: What do you do on weekends?
What did you eat for lunch?
What are you going to do on the weekend?

grammar.explanation:
무슨 always comes directly before a noun: 무슨 음식 (what food), 무슨 요일 (what day of the week). It can't stand alone. To ask "what?" by itself, use 뭐.

무슨 + noun works like any noun phrase and takes whatever particle the noun needs: 무슨 영화를 봤어요? (object), 무슨 색을 좋아해요? (object), 무슨 일이에요? (with 이다; "What's going on?").

무슨 asks what something is out of an open range of possibilities. To choose from a known set, use 어느. To ask what something is like, use 어떤. In many everyday questions 무슨 and 어떤 are interchangeable.

examples.en: What day of the week is it today?

grammar.explanation:
어떤 comes before a noun, like 무슨, but it focuses on qualities: "what kind of ___?", "what is it like?" 어떤 사람이 좋아요? asks about the type of person, such as kind or funny. Answer with an adjective + noun: 친절한 사람이 좋아요.

어떤 is 어떻다 + ~ㄴ, the same way 이런, 그런 and 저런 come from 이렇다, 그렇다 and 저렇다 (Lesson 23).

It can also mean "which" when picking from options. In a statement, without question intonation, 어떤 means "a certain" or "some": 어떤 사람 (someone, a certain person).

examples.en: What kind of person do you like?
What kind of music do you listen to?
examples.note: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣 + 어요 → 들어요.

grammar.explanation:
어느 means "which" when choosing from a set that both people know: countries, directions, the items in front of you. It always goes before a noun: 어느 나라 (which country), 어느 쪽 (which way), 어느 회사 (which company).

어느 것 (which one) is shortened to 어느 거 in speech, and with ~이/가 it becomes 어느 게: 어느 게 더 좋아요?

Compare the three: 무슨 영화 = what movie (any at all); 어느 영화 = which movie (of these); 어떤 영화 = what kind of movie.

examples.en: Which seat do you want to sit in?
Which company do you work at?

grammar.explanation:
몇 means "how many" and goes where a number would go, right before a counter: 사과 세 개 → 사과 몇 개? 학생 다섯 명 → 학생 몇 명?

Answer with the number system that the counter normally uses: 몇 살이에요? → 스무 살이에요 (pure Korean); 몇 층이에요? → 삼 층이에요 (Sino-Korean). Common questions: 몇 시 (what time), 몇 번 (what number, how many times), 몇 월 (what month).

The date question is spelled 며칠, never 몇 일. It means both "what date" and "how many days". Without question intonation, 몇 can also mean "a few": 몇 명이 왔어요 can mean "a few people came".

examples.en: How many apples did you buy?
For how many days did you travel?
How many people are in your family?

grammar.explanation:
얼마나 asks "how much" or "to what degree". Put it right before the verb or adjective: 얼마나 기다렸어요? (How long did you wait?), 얼마나 비싸요? (How expensive is it?). With adjectives it matches English "how + adjective": 얼마나 커요? (how big), 얼마나 멀어요? (how far).

For time taken, 얼마나 걸려요? (How long does it take?) is a very common question. 얼마나 자주 means "how often".

Don't mix it up with 얼마. 얼마 is a noun for price: 이거 얼마예요? (How much is this?). 얼마나 is the adverb for amount or degree.

examples.en: How much did you study Korean?
How long does it take to get to school?
How far is your house from here?

grammar.explanation:
When a question word is the subject (누가, 뭐가, 어디가, 어느 게), it takes ~이/가, never ~은/는. ~은/는 marks something already known, and a question word is by definition unknown. So 누구는 왔어요? is wrong; say 누가 왔어요?

The answer keeps ~이/가 on the part that answers the question, because that's the new information: 누가 왔어요? → 민수가 왔어요. Answering 민수는 왔어요 would suggest a contrast, as if to say others didn't come.

Parts of the sentence that are already known can still take ~은/는: 이 식당에서는 뭐가 제일 맛있어요?

examples.en: This kimchi is the most delicious.

examples.note: The answer keeps ~이/가 because it gives the new information.

lessons.title: Lesson 23: ㅎ Irregular: Korean Colors, 이렇다, 그렇다 and 저렇다

vocab.en: to be revealed, to be shown

grammar.explanation:
Adjectives whose stem ends in ㅎ are irregular. This covers the color words 빨갛다, 노랗다, 파랗다, 하얗다, 까맣다, as well as 이렇다, 그렇다, 저렇다 and 어떻다. 좋다 is the big exception and stays regular (좋아요, 좋은).

Before ~아/어: the ㅎ drops and the vowel merges into ㅐ. 빨갛 + 아요 → 빨개요; 파랗다 → 파래요; 그렇다 → 그래요. A ㅑ stem gives ㅒ: 하얗 + 아요 → 하얘요. The past works the same: 빨갰어요.

Before the modifier ~ㄴ/은: the ㅎ drops and you add ㄴ as if the stem ended in a vowel. 빨갛 + 은 → 빨간; 노랗다 → 노란 사과.

Endings that start with a consonant, such as ~고, ~지 and ~습니다, keep the ㅎ: 빨갛고, 빨갛지 않아요, 빨갛습니다.

examples.note: 빨갛 + 아지다 → 빨개지다: the ㅎ drops before ~아/어.

examples.en: The sky is blue and the clouds are white.
examples.note: 파랗고 keeps the ㅎ because ~고 starts with a consonant.

grammar.explanation:
Korean colors come in two kinds. The five basic colors are adjectives (빨갛다, 노랗다, 파랗다, 하얗다, 까맣다), so they conjugate: 빨개요, 빨간 셔츠. Every color also has a noun form ending in 색 ("color"), which works like any noun.

For the basic five, the noun is the modifier form + 색: 빨간색, 노란색, 파란색, 하얀색, 까만색. Other colors exist only as nouns: 초록색, 보라색, 분홍색, 갈색, 회색, 연두색.

Use the noun with 이다 (셔츠가 회색이에요), as an object (보라색을 좋아해요), or straight before another noun with no particle (분홍색 치마). Before a noun, use the adjective's modifier form: 빨간 치마, never 빨갛다 치마.

So "a red shirt" can be 빨간 셔츠 or 빨간색 셔츠. "It's green" can only be 초록색이에요, because there is no green adjective.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 하얀 셔츠를 입고 있어요.
examples.en: That person is wearing a white shirt.

grammar.point: 이렇다 / 그렇다 / 저렇다 (like this / like that)
grammar.explanation:
These three adjectives match 이, 그 and 저 from Lesson 1. 이렇다 = to be like this (near me, or what I'm about to show). 그렇다 = to be like that (near you, or already mentioned). 저렇다 = to be like that (over there, away from both of us).

Before a noun they take the modifier ~ㄴ, and the ㅎ drops: 이렇 + ㄴ → 이런 ("this kind of"); 그런; 저런. So 이런 셔츠 is "a shirt like this".

With ~게 they become adverbs meaning "in this way": 이렇게, 그렇게, 저렇게. ~게 starts with a consonant, so the ㅎ stays. Before an adjective, they mean "so" or "this much": 그렇게 비싸요? (Is it that expensive?)

examples.en: I want to buy a shirt like this.
I heard a rumor like that.
I want to live in a house like that.
I've never seen such a big dog before.

grammar.explanation:
At the end of a sentence, 이렇다, 그렇다 and 저렇다 conjugate like any ㅎ irregular adjective: 이렇 + 어요 → 이래요; 그래요; 저래요. Past: 그랬어요. They describe a situation as being "like this/that".

그래요 is one of the most common words in Korean conversation. As a statement it means "That's right" or "It is so". As a question, 그래요? means "Really? Is that so?" Casual forms: 그래, 그래?

To politely disagree, use ~지 않다. ~지 starts with a consonant, so the ㅎ stays: 그렇지 않아요 (That's not so). 왜 그래요? asks "What's wrong?" or "Why are you acting like that?"

examples.en: Is the weather always like this?
That person is always like that.

grammar.explanation:
~의 is the possessive particle, like English "'s" or "of": 선생님의 책 (the teacher's book). Attach it to the owner and put the thing owned after it. It has the same shape after vowels and consonants.

In speech, ~의 is usually dropped when the link is obvious: 친구 집 (a friend's house), 우리 엄마 (my mom), 한국 음식 (Korean food). It is kept more in writing, for clarity, and in formal phrases.

저의 and 나의 contract to 제 and 내: 제 지갑 (my wallet), 내 책 (my book, casual). Don't say 저 지갑 for "my wallet"; that means "that wallet over there".

As a particle, 의 is usually pronounced like 에: 선생님의 sounds like [선생니메]. At the start of a word, as in 의자, it keeps the 의 sound.

examples.en: I went to my friend's house.
The teacher's book is on the desk.

examples.note: Two ~의 are dropped here: 저의 → 제, and 친구의 이름 → 친구 이름.
In casual speech, 나의 contracts to 내.

vocab.en: to put, to set, to place something
to be nice, to be kind

grammar.explanation:
전 means "before". After an amount of time it means "ago": 삼 년 전 (three years ago). Like other time words, it usually takes ~에: 삼 년 전에 왔어요.

Build it as number + time unit + 전에: 오 분 전에 (five minutes ago), 이틀 전에 (two days ago), 한 달 전에 (a month ago). Use the same numbers you use for counting time (Lesson 11).

전 can also follow a noun for an event or a clock time: 수업 전에 (before class), 세 시 전에 (before three o'clock). For "just before", use 직전에.

Don't mix it up with 지난: 지난주 means "last week", but 일주일 전에 means "a week ago".

examples.ko: 저는 삼 년 전에 한국에 왔어요.
examples.en: I came to Korea three years ago.
My friend called five minutes ago.
I went to the police station two days ago.
I started exercising a month ago.
I will arrive before three o'clock.

grammar.explanation:
~기 전에 means "before doing". ~기 turns a verb into a noun ("eating", "sleeping"), and 전에 means "before". So 먹기 전에 is literally "before eating".

Add ~기 전에 to the stem, with no change to the stem: 먹다 → 먹기 전에; 자다 → 자기 전에; 공부하다 → 공부하기 전에; 살다 → 살기 전에 (the ㄹ stays).

The ~기 전에 part never takes a tense. Even in the past, say 오기 전에, not 왔기 전에. The tense goes on the final verb: 엄마가 오기 전에 방을 치웠어요.

In two-clause sentences, the subject inside the ~기 전에 part takes ~이/가 (엄마가), and the main subject usually takes ~은/는 (저는).

examples.en: I wash my hands before eating.
I read a book before going to sleep.

examples.ko: 엄마가 오기 전에 저는 방을 치웠어요.
examples.en: Before mom came, I cleaned my room.
Before coming to Korea, I studied Korean.

examples.ko: 출장을 가기 전에 부모님께 전화할 거예요.
examples.en: Before going on my business trip, I'll call my parents.

grammar.explanation:
후 means "after". After an amount of time it means "later" or "from now": 한 시간 후에 (in an hour, an hour later). Like 전, it usually takes ~에.

Build it as number + time unit + 후에: 오 분 후에, 삼 일 후에, 일주일 후에. In speech, 뒤에 is also common: 한 시간 뒤에.

후 can also follow an event noun: 수업 후에 (after class). For "right after", use 직후에.

The final verb decides whether it's past or future: 일주일 후에 만나요 (Let's meet in a week); 일주일 후에 다시 만났어요 (We met again a week later).

examples.en: I go on a business trip in three days.
I go to the library after class.
We met again a week later.

grammar.explanation:
For "after doing", don't use ~기. Use the past modifier ~ㄴ/은 and then 후에. Literally it's "after the having-done".

After a vowel stem, add ~ㄴ 후에: 하다 → 한 후에; 끝나다 → 끝난 후에. After a consonant stem, add ~은 후에: 먹다 → 먹은 후에; 씻다 → 씻은 후에. A ㄹ stem drops the ㄹ: 만들다 → 만든 후에. ㄷ irregulars change: 듣다 → 들은 후에.

Like ~기 전에, this part takes no tense of its own; the final verb carries it. 다음에 or 뒤에 can replace 후에 with the same meaning, and 다음에 is very common in speech.

A common mistake is 먹기 후에. Remember the pair: before = ~기 전에, after = ~ㄴ/은 후에.

examples.en: After taking a bath, I slept.
After class ended, I met a friend.
After eating, I had some snacks.

examples.ko: 숙제를 끝낸 후에 게임을 할 거예요.
examples.en: After I finish my homework, I'll play a game.

examples.ko: 그 노래를 들은 후에 기분이 좋아졌어요.
examples.en: After listening to that song, I felt better.
examples.note: 듣다 is ㄷ irregular: 듣 + 은 → 들은.

examples.en: After making the cake, I cleaned the kitchen.
examples.note: 만들다 drops ㄹ: 만들 + ㄴ → 만든.

grammar.explanation:
~ㄴ/은 이래로 means "since (doing)". It describes something that started at that point and is still continuing. Build it exactly like ~ㄴ/은 후에: 졸업하다 → 졸업한 이래로; 시작하다 → 시작한 이래로; 먹다 → 먹은 이래로.

It can also follow a time noun directly: 작년 이래로 (since last year). The main clause usually describes an ongoing situation, often with ~고 있다, or a change, such as 늘었어요.

이래로 is formal and mostly written. In everyday speech, Koreans tend to use 부터 with a time word, or ~ㄴ/은 후에 with a verb: 작년부터 한국에서 살고 있어요.

examples.ko: 대학교를 졸업한 이래로 이 회사에서 일하고 있어요.
examples.en: Since graduating from university, I have been working at this company.
Since I started exercising, my muscles have grown.
I have been living in Korea since last year.

examples.ko: 한국에 온 이래로 김치를 매일 먹어요.
examples.en: Since coming to Korea, I eat kimchi every day.
I've been living in Korea since last year.
examples.note: This is the everyday spoken way to say 작년 이래로.

grammar.explanation:
안 means "inside". After an amount of time, 안에 means "within": 한 시간 안에 (within an hour). 이내에 means the same but sounds formal; you'll see it on notices, forms and instructions: 일주일 이내에.

Build it as number + time unit + 안에 (or 이내에): 십 분 안에, 이틀 안에, 삼 일 이내에.

Compare with 동안 (Lesson 11): 한 시간 동안 = for an hour (the whole time); 한 시간 안에 = within an hour (sometime before the hour is up). And 한 시간 후에 = an hour from now.

examples.ko: 한 시간 안에 숙제를 끝낼 거예요.
examples.en: I will finish my homework within an hour.
I will arrive within ten minutes.
I paid the bill within a week.

examples.ko: 이틀 안에 이 책을 읽을 거예요.
examples.en: I'll read this book within two days.

examples.note: 동안 means for the whole period; 안에 means before the period is up.

lessons.title: Lesson 25: Anybody, Everybody, Somebody, Nobody, etc.

vocab.en: any time at all (any old time)
to go out with, to date
to be severe, to be extreme

grammar.explanation:
모든 means "every" or "all". It always comes right before a noun: 모든 학생 (every student), 모든 것 (everything). It can't stand alone.

A question word + ~나 makes an "every" word: 어디 + 나 → 어디나 (everywhere); 언제 + 나 → 언제나 (always, every time); 누구 + 나 → 누구나 (everyone, anyone). These normally go in positive sentences: 누구나 알아요 (everyone knows).

모든 vs 모두: 모든 goes before a noun, while 모두 (and casual 다) are adverbs meaning "all" and go before the verb: 학생들이 모두 왔어요 (the students all came).

examples.en: In Korea there are convenience stores everywhere.

examples.note: 모두 goes before the verb; 모든 goes before a noun.

grammar.explanation:
A question word + ~ㄴ가 makes a "some" word, used when something exists but is unknown or unimportant: 뭐 → 뭔가 (something); 어디 → 어딘가 (somewhere); 언제 → 언젠가 (someday); 누구 → 누군가 (someone).

They work like nouns and can take particles (누군가가, 뭔가를, 어딘가에), but in speech the particle is often dropped: 누군가 문을 열었어요.

Don't mix them up with questions. 누가 왔어요? asks "Who came?", but 누군가 왔어요 says "Someone came." 뭔가 before an adjective means "something (about it)": 뭔가 이상해요.

examples.en: I want to go to Korea someday.
I can hear music from somewhere.

grammar.explanation:
아무 + ~나 means "any ___ at all", with the feeling "it doesn't matter which". Use it in positive sentences for offers, permission and choices: 아무 데나 앉으세요 (Sit anywhere you like).

The pattern is 아무 + noun + (이)나: 아무나 (anyone); 아무 거나 (anything, from 아무 것 + 이나); 아무 데나 (anywhere; 데 means place); 아무 때나 (any time; 때 means time). It works with other nouns too: 아무 노래나 (any song).

Compare 누구나 and 아무나. 누구나 means "everyone, all people" (누구나 알아요 = everyone knows). 아무나 means "anyone, no matter who", and can suggest "just anybody".

examples.note: 아무 + noun + (이)나 works with any noun: 아무 노래나.

grammar.explanation:
아무 + ~도 + a negative verb makes "no" words: 아무도 (nobody), 아무 것도 (nothing), 아무 데도 (nowhere). Literally it's "not even any ___".

The verb must be negative: use 안, 못, ~지 않다, 없다 or 모르다. 아무도 왔어요 is wrong; say 아무도 안 왔어요. English uses one negative ("Nobody came"), but Korean needs both 아무도 and 안.

아무도 replaces ~이/가 and ~을/를: 아무도 없어요 (nobody is here); 아무도 안 만났어요 (I didn't meet anyone). Other particles go before 도: 아무한테도 (to nobody), 아무 데에도 or 아무 데도 (nowhere).

Compare: 아무나 = anyone (positive) vs 아무도 = nobody (with a negative).

examples.en: I didn't go anywhere on the weekend.

examples.note: Particles like 한테 go between 아무 and 도.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 아무 데도 못 가요.

grammar.explanation:
~마다 attaches to a noun to mean "every ___" or "each ___". It has the same shape after vowels and consonants: 날 → 날마다 (every day); 주말 → 주말마다 (every weekend); 사람 → 사람마다 (each person).

With time words it shows regular repetition: 아침마다 (every morning), 일요일마다 (every Sunday). With a number + time unit it gives the interval: 십 분마다 (every ten minutes), 두 시간마다 (every two hours).

With other nouns it often means "each one, differently": 사람마다 달라요 (it differs from person to person), 나라마다 (in each country).

examples.en: I go for a walk every day.
I go to my hometown every weekend.
The bus comes every ten minutes.
I call my parents every Sunday.
